title: Migration to Abyssinia
hookLine: a band of persecuted believers flee across the sea to a just Christian king, and Ja'far recites Surah Maryam before him

lines: A KING UNDER WHOM NO ONE IS WRONGED.
cards: Beaten, starved, locked up: that's Mecca now for believers with no powerful family to protect them. And the Prophet ﷺ tells some of them: go. Cross the sea to Abyssinia, in East Africa.
There's a king there, he says, under whom no one is wronged. So small groups slip down to the coast, onto boats, across the Red Sea.
Refugees, families with children, among them his own daughter Ruqayyah, and his cousin Ja'far, 'Ali's brother. In a Christian kingdom, they can pray in peace.
Then a delegation from Mecca arrives, carrying expensive gifts for the king.

teach.b: The delegation asks the king, the Najashi, the Negus, to hand the refugees back. He says: I won't hand over people who came to me for shelter until I've heard them.
The account, told by Umm Salamah, who was there, is preserved in Ibn Ishaq and in the Musnad of Ahmad.

teach.h: JA'FAR: WHO WE WERE, WHO WE ARE.
teach.b: The Muslims choose Ja'far to speak. We were a people in ignorance, he says, worshiping idols, cutting family ties, the strong eating up the weak.

Then Allah sent us a messenger from among us, whose honesty we knew, and he told us to worship One God, to speak the truth, keep trusts, be good to our relatives and neighbors, and stop harming one another.
The king asks: do you have anything of what he brought?

teach.h: SURAH MARYAM, AND THE KING WEEPS.
teach.b: Ja'far recites from the opening of Surah Maryam. After its opening letters, in Pickthall's words: “A mention of the mercy of thy Lord unto His servant Zachariah.”

It's the surah of nida'an khafiyya, of Maryam, an-nakhlah and the baby in the cradle, from week eleven of this path. The account says the king wept until his beard was wet, and the bishops around him wept too.
And he said: this, and what Isa brought, come from the same source of light.

teach.h: I WILL NOT GIVE YOU UP.
teach.b: Go in peace; I won't give you up. The delegation went home with their gifts. The Muslims stayed for years.
When the Negus died, the Prophet ﷺ led a funeral prayer for him in Medina, far away, as a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports.
Muslims remember him with deep gratitude: a Christian king who protected strangers because it was just.

how: Muslims remember the migration to Abyssinia as the first hijra and honor the Negus as a just ruler; the story is often told as an early example of friendship between Muslims and Christians.

games.q: you're the Negus. envoys from Mecca bring you rich gifts and ask you to hand back some refugees who've come to your kingdom. what do you do?
o: take the gifts and hand them over.
send them all away, both sides.
games.why: he calls the refugees to speak, hears Ja'far recite Surah Maryam, weeps, and refuses to give them up.

practice: Think of someone near you who is new, or far from home: a family who just moved in, a colleague still learning the language, a student from another country.
Picture where they sit and who doesn't talk to them, then one small way to make room: a greeting by name, an invitation, a question about where they're from, and real listening to the answer.
If you pray, you can ask Allah to protect them.

wordCard.voice: Najashi. The Christian king of Abyssinia who sheltered the persecuted believers and refused to hand them back.

orig.note: Arabic: the Najashi, the title of the king of Abyssinia (the Negus).

carryVoice: Your line: a just king. Tomorrow, a year of two great losses. That's day ninety-two.
